unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Facilities for Exporters and Importers

facts.statement: Remittances against imports should be completed not later than six months from the date of shipment, except where amounts are withheld towards guarantee of performance; authorised dealers may permit settlement of dues delayed by disputes or financial difficulties, with interest on delayed payments or usance bills payable only for a period of up to three years from the date of shipment.

An authorised dealer may grant extension of time for settlement of import dues up to six months at a time (maximum three years), irrespective of invoice value, for delays on account of disputes about quantity or quality or non-fulfilment of contract terms, financial difficulties, or where the importer has filed suit against the seller. It must ensure the import transactions are not under investigation by the Enforcement Directorate, CBI or other agencies, and, for extension beyond one year from the date of remittance, that the importer's total outstanding does not exceed USD one million or 10 per cent of average import remittances in the preceding two financial years, whichever is lower. Cases beyond these limits go to the Regional Office of the Reserve Bank, and the extension is reported in IDPMS.

An authorised dealer may allow advance remittance for import of goods without any ceiling on these conditions: if the advance exceeds USD 200,000, an unconditional irrevocable standby letter of credit or a guarantee from an international bank of repute abroad, or from an authorised dealer in India issued against the counter-guarantee of such a bank, must be obtained; where the importer (other than a public sector company or government department) cannot obtain such a guarantee and the bank is satisfied about its track record and bona fides, the guarantee need not be insisted on for advance remittances up to USD 5,000,000, under a policy approved by the bank's Board; a public sector company or government department that cannot obtain the guarantee needs a specific waiver from the Ministry of Finance before remitting more than USD 100,000. The bank creates an Outward Remittance Message (ORM) in IDPMS for every such remittance.

In lieu of the exchange control copy of the bill of entry, an authorised dealer may accept a certificate from the CEO or auditor that the goods were imported, if the foreign exchange remitted is less than USD 1,000,000 and the importer is a company listed in India with net worth of not less than Rs 100 crore at its last audited balance sheet, or a public sector company or government undertaking; the facility may be extended to autonomous bodies audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General. For imports at EDI ports the bill of entry is downloaded from the BoE Master in IDPMS, and the bank creates an ORM.

The authorised dealer may allow payment of interest on usance import bills or overdue interest on delayed payments for a period of less than three years from the date of shipment at the rate prescribed for trade credit; on prepayment of a usance import bill, the remittance is made after reducing the proportionate interest for the unexpired portion of usance.

Any deferred payment arrangement, including suppliers' and buyers' credit, for up to three years in the case of import of capital goods and up to one year or the operating cycle, whichever is less, in the case of non-capital goods is treated as a trade credit, for which the procedural guidelines of the Master Direction on External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits and Structured Obligations are followed.

Import finance includes import letters of credit on usance terms, under which the importer gets credit from the overseas supplier on the strength of the bank's credibility, and import loans against imported raw materials or goods for trading, secured by pledge or hypothecation. Supplier's credit is credit extended directly by the overseas supplier to the importer; buyer's credit is credit arranged by the importer from a bank or financial institution outside India to pay for imports, so the supplier is paid on immediate terms. The Import Data Processing and Monitoring System (IDPMS), implemented from 10 October 2016, is a common platform of customs, RBI and banks: customs data from the bill of entry flows to the IDPMS server and on to the bank by AD code, the bank records each activity (document submission, outward remittance data) in real time, and a separate Bill of Entry statement is no longer filed. Importers need an IEC and the goods must be freely importable or covered by a licence.

The courseware states that the maximum supplier's credit or buyer's credit per import transaction that banks can approve is USD 50 million, and gives all-in-cost ceilings for foreign currency trade credit (a widely accepted benchmark of six-month tenor plus 300 basis points for new credits, 350 for existing credits transitioned from LIBOR) and an INR trade credit framework (up to USD 50 million equivalent per transaction, maximum three years of guarantee or comfort).

payload.title: Paying for imports on time: the six-month rule and interest
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Standard rule**: the importer should **complete remittance within six months of the date of shipment**, unless money is **withheld as a performance guarantee**.

**When payment is late**: the bank may permit settlement of dues **delayed by disputes or financial difficulties**. **Interest** on delayed payments or usance bills may be paid only for **less than three years from the shipment date**, at the **rate prescribed for trade credit**.

**Prepaying a usance bill**: the remittance is made **after deducting the interest for the unexpired part** of the usance.

payload.title: Extending the time to pay an import bill: the import version of the rule
payload.core_explanation_md:
An importer who cannot pay on time may ask the bank for an **extension**. The bank can grant **up to six months at a time**, to a **maximum of three years**, whatever the invoice value, if the delay is due to **disputes** about quantity or quality, **financial difficulty**, or a **suit** against the seller.

**Checks**: the invoices are **not under investigation** by the Enforcement Directorate, CBI or others; and, for an extension **beyond one year from remittance**, the importer's **total outstanding** must not exceed **USD 1 million or 10% of average import remittances over the previous two financial years, whichever is lower**.

Compare with exporters: the export test is **whichever is higher** (USD 1 million or 10% of three years' realisations). The import test is **whichever is lower**, over **two** years. **Beyond the limits**: the bank refers to the **RBI Regional Office**. Every extension is **reported in IDPMS**.

payload.title: Paying a supplier in advance: when a guarantee is needed
payload.core_explanation_md:
A bank may allow an **advance remittance for imports without any overall ceiling**, on these conditions:

- **Up to USD 2,00,000**: no guarantee.
- **Above USD 2,00,000**: an **unconditional, irrevocable standby letter of credit** or a **guarantee** from an international bank of repute (or from an Indian bank issued against that bank's counter-guarantee).
- **Exception for private importers**: if the importer **cannot** get the guarantee and the bank is satisfied about its **track record and bona fides**, the guarantee **need not be insisted on up to USD 5 million**, under a **Board-approved policy**.
- **Public sector and government bodies**: a **specific waiver from the Ministry of Finance** is needed before remitting **more than USD 1,00,000** without a guarantee.

The bank creates an **ORM** in IDPMS for **every** such remittance.

payload.title: When a CEO's certificate can replace the bill of entry
payload.core_explanation_md:
Normally the importer shows the **exchange control copy of the bill of entry**. In place of it a bank may accept a **certificate from the CEO or auditor** that the goods have really been imported, **if both** hold:

- **less than USD 10,00,000** (one million) was remitted; and
- the importer is a **listed company with net worth of at least ₹100 crore** at its last audited balance sheet, **or** a **public sector company** or government undertaking.

The facility can also be extended to **autonomous bodies audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General**, such as scientific bodies and academic institutions. At **EDI ports** the bank downloads the bill of entry from the **BoE Master in IDPMS** and creates an **ORM**.

payload.title: Financing imports, and the system that tracks them
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Import letter of credit (usance)**: the importer gets **credit from the supplier** on the strength of the **bank's credibility**.

**Import loan**: a loan against **imported raw material or goods for trading**, secured by **pledge or hypothecation**; importers use them even at higher rates, waiting for prices to rise or the rupee to fall.

**Supplier's credit** vs **buyer's credit**
- **Supplier's credit**: **the overseas supplier** lends directly to the importer.
- **Buyer's credit**: the **importer arranges** a loan from a **bank or institution abroad** to pay the supplier **on immediate terms**.

**IDPMS (Import Data Processing and Monitoring System)**, in use from **10 October 2016**: customs, RBI and banks share one platform. **Customs data from the bill of entry** flows to the system and on to the bank **by its AD code**. The bank records **each step** (document submission, remittance data) **in real time**. **No separate Bill of Entry statement** is filed.

payload.title: Trade credit: how long it may last
payload.core_explanation_md:
Any **deferred payment arrangement** for imports, including **supplier's and buyer's credit**, is a **trade credit** if it runs for:

- up to **three years** for **capital goods**; or
- up to **one year or the operating cycle, whichever is shorter**, for **non-capital goods**.

Trade credits follow the **Master Direction on External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits and Structured Obligations**, not the ordinary import payment rules.

(How much a bank may approve per import, and what the **all-in cost** may be, are set in that Master Direction. Those figures have moved with the LIBOR transition and are not tested here.)

payload.title: Can the bank extend this import bill?
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: goods are shipped on 15 March 2026. The importer does not pay and a dispute about quality follows. Later, the importer asks for an extension beyond one year from the remittance date. Its total outstanding is USD 1,400,000, and its average import remittances over the preceding two financial years were USD 18,000,000. What is the standard payment deadline, and can the bank extend beyond one year?

worked_steps.description: Standard deadline: six months from the date of shipment.
10% of average import remittances over the preceding two financial years.
The limit is the lower of USD 1 million and that 10%.
Compare the outstanding with the limit.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The standard deadline is 15 September 2026. Beyond one year the bank cannot extend: the outstanding exceeds the limit of USD 1,000,000 by USD 400,000, so the case must go to the RBI Regional Office

self_check.prompt_text: If the same importer's average remittances had been USD 8,000,000, what would the limit be?
self_check.expected_takeaway: USD 800,000 (10% of 8 million, which is lower than USD 1 million).

payload.title: Trade credit amounts and all-in cost (held back)
payload.core_explanation_md: The courseware gives these figures for trade credit: the **maximum per import transaction** that banks can approve is **USD 50 million**; the **all-in cost** of foreign currency trade credit is capped at a **six-month benchmark rate plus 300 basis points** for new credits (350 for existing credits moved from LIBOR); and **INR trade credit** may go up to **USD 50 million equivalent** per transaction with a **three-year** maximum for guarantees and comfort letters.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two limits does a bank check before approving a trade credit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The per-transaction amount and the all-in cost ceiling, set in the trade credit directions.

unresolved: The RBI Import Master Direction (updated 12 January 2026) is superseded from 1 October 2026 by RBI's directions of 16 January 2026; the sections taught were in force at the 30 June 2026 cut-off and the new text was not retrieved.

Trade credit amounts (USD 50 million per transaction) and all-in-cost ceilings (benchmark plus 300 or 350 basis points) are in the Master Direction on External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits and Structured Obligations, not retrieved here; the card and question stating them are drafted but held back. They are expected to be resolved when unit 6 (ECBs) is authored from that Master Direction.

The courseware's details for advance remittance beyond those in the Master Direction (import licence on the negative list, remittance direct to the supplier, six months or three years for physical import, fifteen days for evidence; printed p. 154) are not all in the general part of the Master Direction fetched and are not taught.

The courseware's requirement for monitoring through the LC register and remittance register (printed p. 155) and its Rs 100 crore net worth relaxation are taught only as the Master Direction states the relaxation.
The foreign trade policy classification of imports (free, restricted, prohibited) is mentioned only briefly.
